bull.argument: NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 results show exceptional scale. Revenue reached $215.9 billion, up 65%, and operating income rose 60% to $130.4 billion. Data Center revenue grew 68%, driven by the major platform shifts toward accelerated computing and AI, while Professional Visualization grew 70% and Automotive grew 39%. Management describes NVIDIA as a data center scale AI infrastructure company, and it is moving Data Center products to a one-year architecture cadence including Rubin. The company is also diversifying its supply chain into the U.S. and Latin America to add resiliency. The filing acknowledges real risks: a $4.5 billion H20 charge, gross margin falling from 75.0% to 71.1%, and heavy reliance on customers' access to energy and capital. Still, the core economics remain very strong, and management is investing in the ecosystem and its own supply capacity to sustain that growth.

claims.claim: Revenue grew 65% to $215.9 billion in fiscal 2026.
claims.quote: Revenue for fiscal year 2026 was $215.9 billion, up 65% from a year ago.

claims.claim: Data Center revenue grew 68%, driven by accelerated computing and AI platform shifts.
claims.quote: Data Center revenue for fiscal year 2026 was up 68% from a year ago. The strong year-on-year growth was driven by the major platform shifts

claims.claim: Operating income rose 60% to $130.4 billion, showing strong profitability at scale.

bear.argument: The bull case rests on headline growth, but the filing shows how fragile that growth is. Management concedes that demand depends on customers' access to data centers, energy, and capital, and that expanding energy capacity is 'a complex, multi-year process.' Gross margin fell from 75.0% to 71.1%, and the filing ties part of that decline to a $4.5 billion H20 charge, while the company's own inventory write-downs reduced gross margin by 2.6%. The company has also committed heavily ahead of demand: it invested $17.5 billion in private companies and infrastructure funds, many of them illiquid, and provided $3.5 billion in land, power, and shell guarantees to early-stage companies. Supply commitments are non-cancellable, and the filing warns that if demand is overestimated, the company may be unable to reduce purchase obligations. Export licensing adds further uncertainty: the H200 program has produced no revenue to date, and shipments face a 25% tariff. Revenue that depends on a small set of customers, a one-year product cadence, and government licenses is a risky foundation for a premium valuation.

claims.claim: Customer demand depends on data center, energy, and capital availability that the company does not control, and energy expansion is slow.
claims.quote: Expanding energy capacity to meet demand is a complex, multi-year process involving significant regulatory, technical, and construction challenges.

claims.claim: Gross margin declined materially year over year.
Large non-cancellable commitments and investments could produce losses if demand falls short.
claims.quote: If we inaccurately estimate demand, or our customers change orders, as we have experienced in the past, we may not be able to reduce our supply commitments in time, at the same rate, or at all.

bull.argument: The bear case is right that the filing lists real risks, but it weighs them against a business that is still growing fast. Fiscal 2026 revenue rose 65% to $215.9 billion, and Blackwell represented the majority of Data Center revenue, so demand has been concrete rather than speculative. Gross margin fell 3.9 points, but the filing attributes the decline mainly to the shift from Hopper systems to full-scale Blackwell solutions and to the $4.5 billion H20 charge, not to a loss of pricing power. The $17.5 billion in investments and $3.5 billion in guarantees are real exposures, and the filing says so, but they support building the AI ecosystem that drives demand. The H200 point cuts both ways: no revenue yet means that upside is not in current results, and the company is candid about it. Energy, capital, and customer concentration are genuine dependencies that investors should monitor rather than dismiss. On balance, reported growth and profitability justify a constructive view, with these risks sized explicitly.

claims.claim: Blackwell architectures drove the majority of Data Center revenue, showing demand is concrete.
claims.quote: Our Blackwell architectures represented the majority of our Data Center revenue.

claims.claim: The gross margin decline is attributed largely to the product transition to Blackwell full-scale solutions, not only to pricing.
claims.quote: Gross margin decreased in fiscal year 2026 as our business model transitioned from offering Hopper HGX systems to Blackwell full-scale datacenter solutions.

claims.claim: The H200 licensing program has not yet produced revenue, so it is upside not reflected in results.
claims.quote: To date, we have not generated any revenue under the H200 licensing program

bear.argument: The bull case treats the 3.9-point margin decline as a mix shift, but the filing shows pressure that persists beyond one-time items. Management reports that inventory provisions and related effects cut gross margin by 2.6% in fiscal 2026, up from 2.3% in fiscal 2025, so the drag grew even before the H20 charge is counted. The filing also says the company has had to reduce average selling prices, including through channel pricing programs, which undercuts the claim that pricing power is intact. Purchase obligations are growing, and the filing warns they could become a greater portion of supply, which raises the cost of any demand miss. The $17.5 billion in investments is described as largely illiquid, and the filing concedes the startups may never become profitable. Concentration is also real: management says a significant amount of revenue comes from a limited number of partners and distributors. Strong reported growth does not remove these exposures, and a premium valuation assumes they stay contained.

claims.claim: Inventory provisions are a recurring and growing drag on gross margin, not just a one-time H20 effect.
claims.quote: The net effect on our gross margin from inventory provisions and sales of items previously written down was an unfavorable impact of 2.6% in fiscal year 2026 and 2.3% in fiscal year 2025.

claims.claim: The company has had to cut selling prices, which challenges the claim that pricing power is intact.
claims.quote: We have had to reduce average selling prices, including due to our channel pricing programs

claims.claim: Customers with in-house capabilities could replace the company's products, weakening long-term demand.
claims.quote: Some of our customers have in-house expertise and internal development capabilities similar to some of ours and can use or develop their own solutions to replace those we are providing.

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes, but the bear's evidence is more pointed to the bull's claims: it quantifies the recurring inventory drag (2.6% vs 2.3%), cites price reductions against the pricing-power claim, and surfaces competitive substitution risk. The bull directly answers the margin and investment points with filing language, but its defense that margin decline is mainly mix shift does not fully rebut the recurring inventory-provision drag the bear identified, and it leaves the price-cut evidence largely unaddressed.
